intro: You already have all six tenses; what remains is choosing them on purpose. Präteritum is the tense of written narrative and of the background in stories (Es war spät; sie ging nach Hause) and of formal reports (Die Untersuchung ergab …). Plusquamperfekt marks a step further back within that past (Als sie ankam, hatte er das Haus schon verlassen). Perfekt is the spoken past (Gestern habe ich …) and, in writing, the past that still matters now (Die Preise sind gestiegen – wir müssen reagieren). Präsens covers the present, general truths (Wasser kocht bei 100 Grad), plans with a time adverb (Morgen fahre ich …) and — as a stylistic device — the historical present that makes a narrated moment vivid (Mitternacht. Plötzlich klopft es). Futur I predicts or promises; Futur II guesses about the past (Er wird den Zug verpasst haben) or marks completion by a future point (Bis Freitag werden wir … abgeschlossen haben). A tense change inside a text is never neutral: Präteritum → Präsens signals drama; Präteritum → Perfekt signals the narrator stepping into the present. Noticing these shifts is part of reading a story or a report well.
tips[0].title: Narrative: Präteritum main line, Plusquamperfekt for the step back
tips[0].text: Sie ging nach Hause (line). Sie war müde (background, also Präteritum). Er hatte das Haus schon verlassen (earlier). Keep the main line in one tense; reach back with hatte / war + participle only when the order matters.
tips[0].check.why: The earlier event takes the Plusquamperfekt, and beginnen forms it with haben: hatte begonnen. begann gerade would mean it started at the moment we arrived.

tips[1].title: Perfekt: spoken past, and 'past that still counts'
tips[1].text: Gestern habe ich einen Film gesehen (speech). Die Preise sind stark gestiegen – wir müssen reagieren (writing, present relevance). In a report, the Perfekt for the result and the Präteritum for the procedure is a common and deliberate mix.
tips[1].trap: English "I saw / I have seen" does not map onto Präteritum / Perfekt, not even in writing: German has no aspect contrast here. The choice is register (spoken → Perfekt) and, in writing, stylistic distance (Präteritum) versus present relevance (Perfekt). "Ich habe ihn gestern gesehen" is normal German although English says "I saw him yesterday".
tips[1].check.why: German has no aspect contrast here: the Perfekt is the ordinary spoken past, even with a finished time like gestern.
tips[2].title: Präsens: truths, plans, and drama
tips[2].text: Wasser kocht bei 100 Grad (truth). Morgen fahre ich nach Köln (plan + time word). Mitternacht. Plötzlich klopft es (historical present — switch into it for the climax, switch back after).
tips[2].check.why: The story is told in Präteritum and switches into Präsens at the climax. The other two are a plan with a time word and a general truth.
tips[3].title: Futur I and II
tips[3].text: Futur I: prediction, promise, or a guess about now (Er wird wohl krank sein). Futur II: a guess about the past (Er wird den Zug verpasst haben) or completion by a deadline (Bis Freitag werden wir abgeschlossen haben). Plans with a time word stay in the Präsens.
tips[3].check.why: A guess about the past is Futur II, and einschlafen forms its Perfekt with sein. wird einschlafen would be a guess about the future.
remember[0]: Written story: Präteritum + Plusquamperfekt. Speech / relevance: Perfekt. Truth, plan, drama: Präsens.
remember[1]: A tense switch is a signal — use it once, on purpose.
table.caption: Tense by function
mistakes[0].why: The earlier event needs the Plusquamperfekt.
mistakes[1].why: Plans with a time word take the Präsens; Futur adds emphasis or prediction.
mistakes[2].why: Keep the narrative line in one tense.
hook: Choose tenses on purpose: tell the story in Präteritum, step back with Plusquamperfekt, and jump into Präsens when it gets exciting.
tips[1].check.q: English says “I saw him yesterday.” Is „Ich habe ihn gestern gesehen.“ correct German?
tips[1].check.options[0]: Yes, it is the normal spoken past
tips[1].check.answer: Yes, it is the normal spoken past
